Christo/REUTERS Advertisement At least five people have died and another 41 are missing after a ferry caught fire in Indonesia on Sunday morning, authorities have confirmed. The Mutiara Sentosa 2 ferrywas carrying a total of 271 passengers and crew members from Indonesia's second-largest city, Surabaya in East Java, across the Java Sea to Makassar in South Sulawesi. Search and rescue officials said 225 people had been rescued by Sunday afternoon but that an operation was still ongoing. Some passengers reportedly jumped overboard and were picked up by a nearby ship. Four other vessels were on standby nearby but could not approach because of the risk posed by flammable material on the ferry, officials said. What have Indonesian authorities said? "Based on preliminary reports from the field, passengers are waiting to be evacuated by the vessels in the vicinity of the incident site," said Muhammad Masyhud, a senior official at the Indonesian Ministry of Transportation. "The safety of passengers and crew is our top priority. We are continuously coordinating with all relevant parties to ensure that the evacuation process can proceed quickly, safely, and effectively," he added. The fire, the cause of which remains unclear, was reported by the ship's captain who, according to officials, has not been in contact since. Are shipping accidents common in Indonesia? Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where marine accidents are a regular occurrence, due to a combination of unpredictable weather conditions and lax safety standards. Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Selayar, a small tropical island south of the much larger Sulawesi. At least four people were found dead, and 14 others remained missing until the end of the search operation. Edited by: Rana Taha Don't let the algorithm hide the news. Composite: Guardian Design/Reuters/AP/EPA View image in fullscreen The journalists John Abernathy (top), Estefany Rodríguez (right) and Mario Guevara have all been caught up in Trump’s crackdown. Composite: Guardian Design/Reuters/AP/EPA US immigration Freedom oppressed: the journalists caught up in Trump’s ICE crackdown Media workers are grappling with increasingly volatile press climate in US, with some detained and even deported Banished: Trump’s secret deportation deals What is Trump’s third-country deportation policy? Alice Speri Mon 21 Sep 2026 06.00 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A s hundreds of masked and armed US federal agents besieged the streets of Minneapolis, turning the midwestern city into the frontline of the Trump administration’s unprecedented crackdown on immigration, the independent photographer John Abernathy was documenting one of the protests that had become a daily occurrence when Immigration and Customs Enforcement tackled him. A photograph of him on the ground, pepper spray running down his face, captured the violence with which ICE agents had for weeks treated immigrants and the thousands of US citizens who had come to their defence. It was also a stark reminder that journalists were not immune to the agency’s aggressive tactics. The US Press Freedom Tracker documented an increasingly volatile climate for journalists across the country in 2025, reporting 32 arrests and 170 assaults, most of them during protests . And things are no better this year. Journalists who are themselves immigrants have at times also become targets of the hardline policy. Estefany Rodríguez , a Colombian reporter covering immigration for a Spanish-language outlet in Nashville, Tennessee, was arrested in March and held in ICE detention centres in Louisiana and Alabama for two weeks, before a judge ordered her release. Rodríguez had reported on immigration arrests at a local courthouse a day before agents surrounded her car, which was marked with her outlet’s logo, and arrested her. View image in fullscreen An ICE agent raises a finger during an immigration raid in Minneapolis, Minnesota, in January. Photograph: Leah Millis/Reuters It was journalists such as Abernathy and Rodríguez who inspired a multi-outlet investigation, involving staff from two dozen newsrooms in 16 countries and coordinated by Forbidden Stories . The project details the secretive deals the Trump administration has struck with third countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America, to take in deportees the US is unable to send to their countries of origin. Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation deals Read more In Georgia, ICE agents arrested Mario Guevara , an Emmy award-winning journalist from El Salvador. He had lived in Atlanta for nearly two decades, running an independent Spanish-language outlet and documenting immigration enforcement operations on TikTok. Guevara was covering a “No Kings” protest in June 2025 at the time of his arrest. He spent more than 100 days in detention, mostly in isolation. “They didn’t want me to hear the stories of other fellow prisoners and that’s why they locked me up alone,” he told Forbidden Stories. Guevara was deported to El Salvador last October, while his wife and children remain in the US. He has continued to report on US immigration enforcement from there and remains convinced he was targeted because of his journalism. “ICE had a personal campaign against me,” he said, noting that agents repeatedly asked him why he insisted on documenting their activities when he was not a US citizen. “ICE arrested and deported me because of my journalistic work, I’m sure.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security rejected Guevara’s claims, saying allegations he was “arrested by ICE or isolated while in detention because he is a journalist are completely FALSE”. The spokesperson said Guevara was arrested by local authorities for obstruction of law enforcement and deported because an immigration judge had issued a final order of removal more than a decade earlier. “If you come to our country and break our laws, we will arrest you and you will NEVER return,” the spokesperson said. Journalists reporting on the impact of the Trump administration’s third-country removal policy have also faced the hostility of some of those countries’ authorities, particularly in countries where press freedom is already severely restricted. Show more In Cameroon’s capital, Yaoundé, last February, four journalists, including three who were on assignment for the Associated Press, were briefly detained while reporting at a state-run compound where African migrants recently deported from the US were being held. The journalists were accused of criminal trespassing and had their equipment and phones confiscated for a week. During questioning, authorities warned them they would be “crushed” and “disappear[ed] without a trace”, one of the group told the Committee to Protect Journalists . Nalova Akua, one of the journalists detained in Cameroon, told Forbidden Stories he believed they had been targeted because they were exposing the impact of a collaboration with the US government that Cameroonian officials would prefer to keep out of public view. Abernathy tossed his camera to another photographer as agents tackled him to the ground in the hope of saving the photographs he had taken, he previously told the Guardian . “It deserves to be seen, what’s going on around here,” he said. Government headquarters (Photo: Guvernul României) Daniela Budu , 13.10.2026, 14:00 In Bucharest, the prime minister designate Luca Niculescu Monday concluded the first round of negotiations with parliamentary parties and groups regarding support for the government, with a deadline on Thursday to present the list of ministers and the governing programme to Parliament. He proposed a political agreement or a mixed formula which, he believes, would be in a better position to implement necessary measures such as the budget adjustment, the endorsement of the 2027 public budget, energy-related actions, economic recovery, and the strengthening of Romania’s defence capabilities. However, he says alternative solutions exist, ranging from a hybrid government to a cabinet of technocrats supported by a six-month political agreement. Luca Niculescu: “I suggested we consider a six-month support agreement, for instance, for priority reforms and key initiatives Romania needs to undertake, and I hope the parties will reach an understanding and work together to find a formula to pull the country out of this political, economic, and social crisis. We have made progress, the situation today is different from a week ago, but we need to pick up the pace.” While the Social Democratic Party (PSD) calls for a governing partnership with the National Liberal Party (PNL) and the Democratic Union of Ethnic Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), the Liberals, led by Ilie Bolojan, strongly reject such an option. Under these circumstances, the PSD president Sorin Grindeanu says his party is seriously considering early elections, even though talks with the prime minister-designate appear to be moving in the right direction: Sorin Grindeanu: “The National Permanent Bureau has voted to set up a committee to look at the election legislation. They must examine the legal framework regarding the possibility of early elections and determine what changes might be necessary. It is not a scenario we desire, and not out of electoral calculation, but we do not shy away from it, and we will be prepared.” Meanwhile, the Liberals stand firm and categorically refuse to join a coalition government with the Social Democrats. The Senate speaker Mircea Abrudean emphasises that the party is willing to vote for the Luca Niculescu cabinet to break the deadlock, but categorically rules out any hybrid arrangement that deviates from established party lines. Mircea Abrudean: “Obviously, this would affect an endorsement vote for the Luca Niculescu government, because the decisions were clear, I do not believe any other course of action is up for discussion if we want to secure a vote from the National Liberal Party.” Given the situation, the prime minister-designate has sought support from other parliamentary parties and groups. Save Romania Union (USR) has once again rejected the idea of ​​supporting a government that includes Social Democratic ministers. For their part, representatives of the UDMR have announced their intention to vote for a government, even if they will not be part of it. Meanwhile, the national minority groups, “Peace First Romania” and “United for Romania,” have voiced support for the new cabinet but are calling for social protection and economic recovery measures.
